node.label: Emma LaRocque
node.date_label: Defeathering the Indian 1975 · dissertation 1999 · When the Other Is Me 2011
node.description: A scholar whose criticism of Canadian historical writing began with school textbooks. Her 1974 research for Alberta found 'endless layers of stereotypes … particularly in history and social studies' and led to Defeathering the Indian (1975). Her 1999 dissertation named its targets. James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing was 'eye-opening and ground-breaking' but 'does not go deep enough', for 'Canadian historiography is not that benign'. Trigger's foreword to Sioui's Autohistory showed 'a language of containment'. The 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk framed 'all things Native' as 'cultural differences'. Scholars, 'especially historians and literary critics', must 'comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization'. She drew on Memmi, Fanon and Said, and on Howard Adams's 'White Ideal'. When the Other Is Me (2011) is the revised book.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Emma LaRocque; Defeathering the Indian (1975); Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices in Canadian Historiography and Literature (PhD, University of Manitoba, 1999); When the Other Is Me: Native Resistance Discourse, 1850–1990 (2011).
node.scope_note: Read: 1999 dissertation, PDF pp. 8, 11, 21, 29, 34, 37–38, 47, 54, 70, 118–119, 135–136, 249. Defeathering the Indian (1975) is catalogue-only; When the Other Is Me (2011) is known through the publisher's description. Her critiques of Walker's survey and of Trigger's foreword are drawn as edges to Indigenous–newcomer historiography by that entry's editors. 17 Canadian History PhDs cite her (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).
